title: Hybrid Orbitals in Water
lead: Pure p orbitals on oxygen would make water's bonds meet at 90°, yet they meet at 104.45°. Hybrids with unequal shares of s and p connect a molecule's measured bond angle to the makeup of its orbitals, lone pairs included.
notes: By Andrew Wolff and Martin (Stackexchange), shared under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the book credits neither its box diagram nor its water drawing, and Figure 10.2.1 is shown as a PNG of the book's BMP.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise in this section. The one here, on ammonia's hybrids, was written by AI with its solution, Bloom level and concept tags.

exercises.prompt: Ammonia's H–N–H bond angle is 106.7°. Treat its three N–H bonding hybrids as equivalent and its lone pair as the fourth hybrid. (a) What is the s character of each N–H hybrid, in percent? (b) Using the rule that the hybrids of one atom share out its one s and three p orbitals, what is the s character of the lone-pair hybrid, in percent?

parts.hint: Equation 10.2.8 gives γ² from the angle; Equation 10.2.7 turns γ² into the s character.
The s characters of the four hybrids add up to 1, as the p characters add up to 3.

answer.solution:
(a) By Equation 10.2.8, $\gamma^2 = -\cos 106.7^\circ = 0.2874$. By Equation 10.2.7 the s character is $\dfrac{\gamma^2}{1+\gamma^2} = \dfrac{0.2874}{1.2874} = 0.223$, about 22.3% (and 77.7% p).

(b) The p characters of the four hybrids add up to 3, so their s characters add up to 1: $3(0.223) + x_s = 1$, giving $x_s = 0.330$, about 33.0%. As in water, the lone pair has more s character than the bonds.

footnotes.html: The book prints this diagram as Figure 10.2.4, the number it also gives the lone-pair picture below. It is carbon's diagram, $2s^2\,2p^2$ promoted to four half-filled $sp^3$ hybrids, where oxygen's $2s^2\,2p^4$ would fill two of the four. Its caption describes the unhybridized model of Equations 10.2.1 and 10.2.2, in which the orbitals left for the lone pairs are $2s$ and $2p_x$, not $2s$ and $2p_z$.
For a pure $sp^3$ hybrid, $\gamma^2 = 1/3$ and $\gamma = 0.577$; 0.25 is its s character, $\gamma^2/(1+\gamma^2)$.
Equation 10.2.7 squares $\gamma^2$ where it should square $\gamma$: $\left(\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\gamma^2}{1+\gamma^2}$.
The bond angle gives $\gamma$ through Equation 10.2.8, $\cos\theta = -\gamma^2$; Equation 10.2.7 then gives the s character.
The p character is 0.80, that is 80%, not 0.80%.
From $1/(1+\gamma^2) = 0.7$, $\gamma^2 = 1/0.7 - 1 = 0.43$, so $\cos\theta = -0.43$ and $\theta = 115°$. The printed $1/(0.7 - 1)$ would give $-3.3$.
Figure 10.2.1's licence is CC BY-NC-SA, printed as CC-SA-BY-NC.

steps.tex: \mk{l}{\langle N ( p + \gamma s) | N ( p + \gamma s) \rangle} = 1

steps.cap: In integral notation, where $d\tau$ represents all space; the orbitals are real.

steps.tex: \mk{pp}{N^2 \int p^2\; d\tau} + \mk{sp}{N^2 2 \gamma \int sp\; d\tau} + \mk{ss}{N^2 \gamma^2 \int s^2 \; d\tau} = 1

assumes.text: The atomic orbitals $p$ and $s$ are each normalized: $\int p^2\,d\tau = \int s^2\,d\tau = 1$.
The atomic orbitals $p$ and $s$ are orthogonal: $\int sp\,d\tau = 0$.

then.tex: \mk{pp}{N^2 \int p^2\; d\tau} + \mk{sp}{N^2 2 \gamma \int sp\; d\tau} + \mk{ss}{N^2 \gamma^2 \int s^2 \; d\tau} = 1

steps.cap: These terms simplify either due to orthogonality or normality of the constitute atomic orbitals.

assumes.text: A $p$ orbital pointing along the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ is $u_x p_x + u_y p_y + u_z p_z$, as the turned orbitals of Section 10.1 are; $p_1$ points along one bond, $p_2$ along the other.
The orbitals $s$, $p_x$, $p_y$ and $p_z$ are normalized and mutually orthogonal.
The two bonds, and so $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$, meet at the bond angle $\theta$.

steps.cap: Each $p_i$ is a sum of $p_x$, $p_y$ and $p_z$, all orthogonal to $s$, so the cross terms vanish.
With orthonormal $p_x$, $p_y$, $p_z$, the overlap of two such orbitals is the dot product of their direction vectors.
